title: gidB and streptomycin
dek: gidB (rv3919c) methylates 16S. Loss-of-function is a common low-level SM resistance route, often phylogenetic or mixed with rpsL. It is not an amikacin call by itself.
story: Streptomycin resistance in MTBC is classically rpsL (K43R, K88R) for high-level, rrs for some alleles, and gidB loss-of-function for low-level. GidB is a 7-methylguanosine methyltransferase acting on 16S rRNA. Frameshifts and nonsense in gidB raise SM MIC modestly. Many are lineage-associated or arise repeatedly because the gene is dispensable in vitro.

WHO catalogue grading of gidB is a cautionary tale: not every indel is a high-confidence SM-R for therapy, and SM is already a historical drug. Do not import a gidB frameshift into an amikacin decision. AMK cares about rrs 1401 and friends; eis promoter is KAN-biased.
If a genome is rpsL K43R, you do not need gidB to explain SM-R. If only gidB is hit, write low-level SM and keep AMK reasoning separate.
deep: Some lineages carry gidB polymorphisms that older pipelines over-called.
Heteroresistant rpsL plus gidB WT is still high-level SM-R in the subpopulation.
SM in retreatment “Category II” is retired. This plate exists so you do not resurrect it from a BAM.
tlyA is the capreomycin methyltransferase story, not gidB.

visual.caption: Split the aminoglycoside genome: rpsL/gidB for SM, rrs 1401 for AMK, eis/whiB7 for KAN, tlyA for CAP.

example.setup: Pipeline flags gidB as “aminoglycoside resistance.” Clinic withholds AMK from a salvage recipe that needed it.

steps.title: Read the gene
steps.body: gidB is SM-tilted. Check rrs 1401 for AMK.

steps.body: If you are here, you are in salvage. Name AMK correctly.

example.takeaway: gidB explains streptomycin, not the whole injectable class.
